name: Head shaving

lead: Head shaving removes all scalp hair for a uniform clean look. People with thinning or receding hair often use it so the hairline stops being a focus, and others choose it simply as a style.
It has a long cultural history, and shaving by people with hair loss has become much more accepted since the 1990s.

paras: Done with clippers or a razor, often repeated every few days. Looksmax.org members post before-and-after photos and ask for opinions.
Nicks, razor irritation and sun exposure on the scalp. Forum users report mixed reactions to the look.

angle.text: Shaving removes thinning or uneven hair so the scalp looks uniform, which hides a receding hairline or patchy loss and puts attention on head shape, skull and facial structure. Forum posts stress that the result depends on facial features, neck and physique.

lead: Head shaving is the removal of all scalp hair, usually with clippers or a razor, for aesthetic, practical, cultural or religious reasons; it is also called going bald by choice.[1] For people whose hair is thinning or receding, it replaces an uneven hairline with a uniform, clean look, so attention moves from the hair to head shape, face and physique. Shaving by people with alopecia areata or pattern hair loss has become much more common and socially accepted since the 1990s.[1]

Shaved heads are often read in popular culture as stern, disciplined or hardcore, and film and television characters from Yul Brynner's King of Siam to Walter White have reinforced that image.[1][2] Looksmax.org members post shaved-head photos for opinions, and the replies tend to focus on head shape, neck, weight and body, with one poster remarking that the look needs a strong build to carry it.[3][4]

Head shaving has a long history in religious ordination, military induction, sport and fundraising, and in the 2020 lockdowns many men shaved their own heads when barbershops closed.[1] No clinical trial has tested head shaving as an appearance intervention; research that mentions it concerns medical settings, ritual practices and perception studies of shaved men.[5][6][7]

paras: The style ranges from a close clipper cut to a razor-smooth scalp. Wikipedia lists aesthetics, convenience, fashion, practicality, punishment, rites of passage, religion and style among the reasons people shave.[1] For people with hair loss it is one of the commonest ways to present a clean head; the other medical reasons it names are lice prevention and chemotherapy-related hair loss.[1]
Women shave less often, and the look then tends to be read as androgynous, according to the same article.[1]

The earliest records come from Egypt, Greece and Rome. Romans offered a person's first shave to the gods, a custom probably borrowed from Greece, and in ancient Greece and much of Babylon a shaved head marked a slave while long hair signified status.[1] Most Buddhist monks and nuns, and some Hindu ones, shave on entering their order, Hare Krishna devotees shave, and Muslim men may shave after Umrah or Hajj.[1] The Christian tonsure is a ritual partial shave of the head in religious orders.[1]

Shaving is widespread in militaries, justified by hygiene and by an image of discipline and conformity, and for recruits it can be a rite of passage.[1] Prisoners are often shaved to prevent lice, though it has also been used as punishment, as when thousands of French women were shaved in public after World War II.[1] Competitive swimmers and sprinters sometimes shave the whole body to reduce drag.[1]

Actor Yul Brynner shaved his head in 1951 for The King and I and kept it shaved for life; the style became known as the Yul Brynner look and some fans imitated it.[2] Wikipedia lists later screen figures such as Vin Diesel, Samuel L. Jackson and Bruce Willis among bald characters read as stern or hardcore.[1]

Skinheads emerged among working-class youth in London in the late 1960s, drawing on mod and Jamaican rude boy fashion; cropped hair became their defining feature by the early 1970s, and the Oi! revival of the late 1970s spread fully shaved heads.[1][8] Head shaving also appears in hardcore, metal, hip hop and techno scenes.[1]

Chemotherapy hair loss is a well-known side effect, and some people shave their heads before treatment or in solidarity, often to raise funds, as in St. Baldrick's events.[1] In 2020, lockdowns closed barbershops and many men shaved their heads, and a UK Covhead-19 challenge on JustGiving aimed to raise funds for the NHS.[1]

Grokipedia reports a 2012 Wharton School study by Albert Mannes in which men with fully shaved heads were rated as more dominant, masculine and confident than men with full hair; this summary was not checked against the original paper.[9] Wikipedia notes the association of a shaved head with authority and virility in popular culture.[1]

Threads share shaved-head photos for rating. Replies mention head shape, weight and neck, and members describe the look as suiting people with a developed physique; one poster who shaved as an experiment later grew his hair back.[3][4]
On T Nation, one poster relayed a partner's preference for shaved heads and a clean-shaven face on men.[10]

Surgeons shave the scalp for some neurosurgical procedures, though a series of 632 craniotomy patients operated without head shaving reported a 1.1 percent postoperative wound infection rate.[5] Ritual shaving has had health implications: a review of the Hajj notes that razor reuse by street barbers can expose pilgrims to hepatitis B or C, and a case report describes ophiasis-pattern alopecia areata in an infant after a head-shaving ritual.[6][7]

Razor nicks, irritation and sunburn on an unprotected scalp are the practical issues discussed around frequent shaving; the sources cited here do not quantify them. The Hajj review's warning concerns shared razors.[6]
No studies found. Related literature covers surgical scalp preparation, shaving rituals and perception of shaved men.[5][6][7][9]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members discuss shaving as a way to handle thinning hair and as a look whose success they say depends on face, neck and body.[3][4]

claims.claim: A shaved head looks good only on people with a strong face and physique.
Shaving a thinning hairline looks better than a visibly receding style.
A shaved head makes men look dominant or aggressive.

timeline.event: In ancient Greece a shaved head is a marker of slavery, per encyclopedic accounts.[1]
Yul Brynner shaves his head for The King and I and keeps the look for life.[2]
Skinhead subculture emerges among London working-class youth; by the early 1970s cropped or shaved hair is its hallmark.[8]
Shaving becomes much more common and accepted among people with alopecia and pattern hair loss.[1]
A series of 632 craniotomies without head shaving is reported with a 1.1 percent wound infection rate.[5]
Barbershop closures during COVID-19 lockdowns prompt many men to shave their own heads.[1]
